quotes.verbatim_quote:
A backdoor dominant is a dominant 7" chord that substitutes the V7
chord for a bVII7 chord approaching the | chord by a whole step. This
works because the bVII7 has a lot of notes in common with an altered
V7 chord.

Example: Bb7-Cmaj/
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the formal definition and rule for the backdoor dominant, a concept that recurs throughout the harmonic analysis of Stella and is essential for understanding other standards.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The ii chord is being added in front of the backdoor dominant. There-
fore, the Bbmin7-Eb7 is really acting as a backdoor ii-V into the Fmaj7.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage defines the backdoor ii-V as distinct from a simple backdoor dominant, giving the reader a reusable harmonic pattern.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
A hybrid ii-V-I is when a minor ii-V-i is mixed with a major ii-V-l. The ii
and V are borrowed from the minor key, but they resolve to the major |.

Example: Dmin7(b5)-G7(b9)-Cmaj7
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the formal definition of the hybrid ii-V-I with a concrete example, a construct the author flags as recurring across many jazz standards.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
This compositional technique
is used to add a sense of surprise. When you hear the minor ii-V being
played, it gives you the sense that it will resolve to a minor chord, but
then unexpectedly, it resolves to a major chord.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage gives the player the listening cue and expressive reason behind the hybrid ii-V-I, essential for both recognition and intentional use when improvising.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
When we come across songs like Stella, it can be beneficial to take a
step back and map out the notes we have available to us. While scales
are not musical by themselves, they can help us conceptualize which
notes we can choose from. From there, we can start to build melodies
and make sense of how to connect the harmony in our lines.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage introduces the Note Choice Map as a systematic pre-improvisation tool, the foundational rationale for the method demonstrated in the chapter.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
One exercise | like to do to keep things simple and help me start to
improvise is create quarter note solos. This means | stick to a quarter
note rhythm in all of my note choices. | take out the rhythmic compo-
nent from my improvisation and just focus on navigating the changes.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This defines the quarter-note solo exercise as a specific practice technique for isolating harmonic navigation from rhythmic complexity, applicable to any difficult standard.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The first thing to note is that we have a series of unresolved ii-V chord
progressions within the first 8 bars. We have seen these before. This
just means the progressions do not resolve to the | chord but move
somewhere else. The key center is being eluded to, yet never comes
home.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This passage defines the rule for how unresolved ii-Vs function, pointing toward a key center without landing, which is the central harmonic device driving Stella's first section.

quotes.topic: Relating roman numerals to parent key
quotes.verbatim_quote:
My strategy here was to re-
late all of the roman numerals back to the parent key while color-cod-
ing what | deemed important to think about as targeting different key
centers.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This states the analytical method used throughout the chapter, anchoring all roman numerals to Bb major regardless of momentary key center.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The Altered Scale and the Lydian Dominant are the ones you haven't
seen before in this book, but | do have them clearly spelled out.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This flags two previously unintroduced scale types required for improvising over Stella, alerting the reader to study them before attempting the note map.
